Whaam!

Roy Lichtenstein’s two-canvas war comic: a fighter plane fires on the left, and the target explodes on the right under the sound effect WHAAM!

Source
Tate: ‘Whaam!’, Roy Lichtenstein, 1963
Creator
Roy Lichtenstein
Made
1963
Style
Pop art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Loud, graphic, ironic
Evidence
Downloaded and inspected Tate’s image of the painting, Tate T00897 (1536 × 660 px), in a scratchpad. No image is stored.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

Tate gives the medium as acrylic paint and oil paint on canvas. Tate.

The diptych was first shown at the Leo Castelli Gallery, New York, in 1963 and bought by the Tate Gallery in 1966. Lichtenstein adapted it from several comic-book panels; the main source is a panel drawn by Irv Novick for a 1962 war comic. Wikipedia.

The exhibition poster for the same 1963 Castelli show is Crak!.

Observed

  • Two canvases side by side, each framed as one comic panel; the thin gap between them acts as a gutter.
  • The sky on both canvases is a field of small, even blue dots on white. The plane’s shadows use a lavender dot tint.
  • Every shape has a black outline of even weight. Clouds, smoke, and flames are closed shapes with flat fills.
  • A yellow caption box with a black outline sits at top left and holds hand-lettered capitals: “I PRESSED THE FIRE CONTROL… AND AHEAD OF ME ROCKETS BLAZED THROUGH THE SKY…”.
  • “WHAAM!” runs down the right canvas in tall yellow slanted capitals with black outlines.
  • The explosion is flat red and yellow with white and black; bundles of black speed lines radiate from it.
  • The rocket trail is a band of parallel red, yellow, and black stripes.

Why it belongs

Whaam! shows every device in the style record at once: dot tints, key lines, a caption box, a sound effect, and speed lines. It is the best single reference for the comic-panel branch.

The dots are used only as tints for sky and shadow. Figures, flames, and lettering stay solid, which keeps the image legible at a distance.

Borrow

Split a hero into two panels with a narrow white gutter, and let one action continue across the gap.

Use one dot tint for the whole background and keep the foreground in solid flat color.

Put a short narration in a yellow outlined caption box in the top corner.
